title: Idempotency Keys and Safe Retries
oneLiner: A timeout doesn't tell the client whether the charge happened. An idempotency key lets it retry anyway without charging twice.
keyTakeaway: When a request times out, the client can't tell whether the server never got it, is still working on it, or finished and the response was lost. Retrying a POST blindly can then charge a card twice. The fix is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique id for each logical operation, sends it with every attempt, and the server records the key with the result, atomically with the work, and answers repeats with the stored result. Claim the key with a unique insert before doing the work so two concurrent attempts can't both run, reject a reused key with a different body, and keep keys for at least as long as clients may retry.
explanation:
Networks fail in an unhelpful way: a client that sends a request and gets no answer can't tell which of three things happened. The request may never have reached the server. The server may still be working on it. Or the server may have finished, charged the card, and lost the response on the way back (a dropped connection, a load balancer timeout, a phone going into a tunnel). For a GET none of this matters, because reading twice is harmless. For POST /charges it matters a great deal: not retrying risks losing a real payment, and retrying risks charging the customer twice. Mobile apps, SDKs and service meshes retry automatically, and users press the button again, so an API that moves money or sends messages has to handle repeats deliberately.

An idempotency key turns a non-idempotent operation into an idempotent one. The client creates a unique value, usually a random UUID (a 128-bit identifier that is practically never generated twice), for each logical operation, such as "pay for basket 881", and sends it in a header on the first attempt and on every retry of that same operation: Idempotency-Key: 5f1c.... The server keeps a table of keys it has seen. On a new key it does the work and stores the key together with the response. On a key it has already completed it does nothing and returns the stored response, the same status code and body as the first time, so the client can't tell a replay from the original. Stripe popularised this pattern, and an IETF draft standardises the Idempotency-Key header. A key is scoped to one account (so two customers can't collide) and has a lifetime: Stripe keeps keys for 24 hours, which must be longer than any client's retry window.

The details are where implementations go wrong. First, concurrency. A client that times out after 2 seconds and retries may send its second attempt while the first is still running. If the server checks "have I seen this key?" and only records it after finishing, both attempts see nothing and both charge. The fix is to claim the key first, with an atomic insert into a table with a unique constraint (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, or a conditional put in DynamoDB) and status "in progress". Whoever inserts it does the work; any other attempt finds an in-progress row and gets 409 Conflict ("still processing, retry shortly") rather than a second charge. Second, atomicity. Saving the result and the key's completion must happen in the same database transaction as the work itself, or a crash between them leaves a charge with no record of it. When the work calls an external system (a card network, an email provider), pass the key, or one derived from it, downstream, so that system deduplicates too. Third, misuse. If a client reuses a key with a different body (another amount), that is a bug, not a retry: store a hash of the request with the key and reject a mismatch with 422 rather than silently replaying the wrong result. Fourth, failures. If the attempt failed with a validation error, the stored 4xx response is replayed; if it failed with a transient server error before doing anything, release the key so a retry can try again. If the worker crashed mid-attempt, its in-progress row would block every retry with 409 until the key expires, so store a lease time (locked_at) with the claim: a retry that finds an expired lease reclaims the row, asks the downstream system about the forwarded key, and only re-runs the work if that system never saw it.

The key belongs to the operation, not the attempt. Generate it when the user starts the action (when the checkout page loads, or when the job is created) and keep it across retries and even app restarts; generating a fresh key per HTTP attempt defeats the whole mechanism.

Sometimes the API can be made naturally idempotent instead. A client-chosen id turns create into PUT: PUT /orders/{client_order_id} creates the order the first time and is a no-op after that. Setting state ("status": "shipped") rather than applying a change repeats safely. Conditional requests (If-Match with an ETag) make an update apply only to the version it was based on. Message consumers do the same with an event id, as in the Message Queues lesson: at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer gives effectively-once processing.

Retries still need the discipline from the Resilience lesson: a few attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, and no retries on 4xx errors other than 409, 429 and 408. Idempotency makes a retry safe; backoff makes it polite.

How the simulator works. A client pays $40 with POST /charges. Pick what goes wrong on the first attempt, whether the client sends an idempotency key, and how the server stores keys. The client times out after 2 seconds and retries up to three times (after a timeout or a 409), with backoff. The log shows each attempt, the server's key table and how many times the card was charged.
